title: Ships Struck Twice in Hormuz as Repeat Attacks Test Tanker Traffic
excerpt: At least six vessels have been hit more than once in two months in the Strait of Hormuz, consultants say. Whether the repeats are deliberate deterrence or the arithmetic of a shrinking target pool is disputed, but traffic through the chokepoint has not stopped.
body:
• At least six commercial ships have been struck more than once in the Strait of Hormuz in October and November, according to security consultancy EOS Risk, in a pattern consultants call "double-tapping".
  • The UAE-owned Navig8 Messi is believed to have been hit three times; the Tara Gas caught fire after strikes on November 16 and 17, and the tanker Gem No 2 spilled oil near the UAE coast after attacks on October 9 and 10.
  • Why the same ships are hit twice is disputed: some shipping executives say fewer ships are using the route, raising the odds of a repeat hit, while others see a deliberate effort to disable vessels and deter traffic.
  • Traffic has not stopped: Lloyd's List counted 237 inbound transits into the Gulf in October, the highest monthly figure since the conflict began, though still below pre-conflict levels.

Attackers in the Strait of Hormuz are hitting the same commercial ships more than once, according to a Financial Times report citing maritime security consultants, in a pattern that is raising the cost and risk of moving oil through the world's most important energy chokepoint.

At least six vessels were struck twice during October and November, according to the security consultancy EOS Risk. The United Arab Emirates-owned vessel Navig8 Messi is believed to have been hit three times, a maritime security adviser told the Financial Times. The Tara Gas was struck on November 16 and again the following day, and subsequently caught fire. The Chinese-owned crude oil tanker Gem No 2 was attacked on October 9 and 10, resulting in a major oil spill near the UAE coastline.

Deliberate deterrence, or a shrinking target pool?

The intent behind the repeat strikes is contested, and the distinction matters for every shipowner deciding whether to transit. Some shipping executives cited by the Financial Times believe the repeats reflect probability: relatively few ships are still using the contested route, so each one faces a higher chance of being hit more than once. Others believe the repeated targeting is deliberate, an attempt to disable vessels and prevent them from returning to service.

What is not in dispute is the effect. Strikes on a ship's stern or machinery can damage propulsion and leave a vessel unable to move; further attacks then complicate emergency response, towing and salvage. The Joint Maritime Information Center's November 26 advisory independently warned that deliberate attacks remained highly likely in the strait, in both eastbound and westbound lanes, and flagged risks to disabled, anchored and slow-moving vessels and to the salvage craft that serve them.

Iran's list, and the traffic that continues

Iran has also expanded its list of vessels it considers non-compliant with its proposed maritime registration arrangements, associated with a proposed Persian Gulf Strait Authority. More than 260 vessels are now on the list, according to the Financial Times, and the majority were added after being attacked, according to maritime intelligence company Windward. Most vessels still transiting favour routes closer to Oman's coastline, with a US naval presence in the area.

Yet traffic has continued, and by one measure recovered. Lloyd's List data cited by the Financial Times showed inbound transits into the Gulf reached 237 in October, the highest monthly figure since the conflict began, driven partly by crude tankers carrying cargoes to ships waiting outside the Gulf near Fujairah. Separate Lloyd's List Intelligence figures recorded 550 non-Iranian-linked transits in October, up from 504 in September. The two series measure traffic differently and are not directly interchangeable, but both point the same way: shipping has not stopped.

Attacks at their highest since the war began

The repeat strikes sit inside a broader escalation. Iran has intensified attacks on tankers in recent weeks: the number of attacks soared in October to the highest level since the war began at the end of February and has continued at a nearly daily pace in November, according to data compiled by Bloomberg and reported by OilPrice.com. This week Iran's Revolutionary Guard said two more tankers hit naval mines on routes it considers unauthorised, setting their engine rooms on fire. Crude volumes flowing through the strait have declined in recent days, although it is unclear how much of that decline the attacks explain.

For Asian buyers, the exposure is direct: China's crude imports rose 11% to 311 million barrels in October, with more than one-third coming from the Gulf, according to commodities data provider Kpler cited by the Financial Times. India, which draws a large share of its crude through the same waterway, faces the same arithmetic. ADNOC declined to comment on individual vessels, and the owners of Tara Gas and Gem No 2 did not respond to requests for comment.

What to watch

The next signals are practical ones: whether the Joint Maritime Information Center's advisories change, whether insurers raise war-risk premiums further.ther for the strait, and whether the October recovery in transits survives November's near-daily attacks. A pattern of repeat strikes, whatever its intent, prices itself into freight and insurance within weeks, and from there into the fuel bills of every economy that buys Gulf crude.
